title: Why 1,000 People Are Enough
objective: After this level you can explain why a random sample of about 1,000 can describe a whole country, whatever its size.
summary: The sample a poll needs depends on the precision wanted, not the population's size. About 1,000 random people give about plus or minus 3 points; more buys little.

cards.headline: Your chance of being in a Pew poll is about 1 in 26,000.
cards.body: Pew's panel has about 10,000 adults, out of about 260 million in the US. Yet its polls speak for all of them. How can so few speak for so many? The answer surprises almost everyone: the size of the country barely matters.

cards.headline: The size of the pot doesn't matter
cards.body: Taste a well-stirred small pot and a well-stirred giant vat: one spoonful tells you about as much in each. Samples work the same way. The sample size you need depends on how precise you want to be, not on how big the population is. The same 1,000 people can represent a population of 100,000 or of 1,000,000.

cards.headline: Bigger helps, then barely
cards.body: Size still matters, just not how you'd guess. The margin of error falls steeply as a sample grows from 100 to 1,000 people. After that it crawls: a random sample of about 1,000 gives about plus or minus 3 points, and doubling from 1,000 to 2,000 cuts it by only about one point. That's why national polls usually ask 1,000 to 2,000 people.

cards.fact: The mix matters more than the size.
cards.context: Remember Level 53: about 2.4 million answers from tilted lists lost to Gallup's far smaller, carefully drawn sample. Randomness buys fairness. Only then does size buy precision, and after about 1,000 people it buys less and less.

questions.prompt: The sample size a poll needs depends mainly on:

options.label: How many people live in the population
How many questions the poll asks
options.rationale: More questions don't change how many people you need.

options.label: How precise the result needs to be
How many pollsters are working on it
options.rationale: Staff numbers don't set the sample size.

questions.explanation: Sample size is a function of the precision wanted, not of population size: 1,000 can serve 100,000 or 1,000,000.

questions.prompt: Match each change in a random sample with what happens to the margin of error.
questions.explanation: As a sample grows from 100 to 1,000 people, the margin falls steeply. A random sample of about 1,000 gives about plus or minus 3 points, and doubling to 2,000 cuts it by only about one point.

questions.prompt: Written as "1 in N", which gives you a bigger chance of being polled?

options.label: 1 in 26,000, because 26,000 is the bigger number of the two
options.rationale: A bigger N means a smaller share.

options.label: They're the same chance
options.rationale: 1 in 2,600 is ten times the chance of 1 in 26,000.

options.label: You can't compare them without percents
options.rationale: Comparing N is enough: smaller N, bigger share.

options.label: 1 in 2,600, because a smaller N means a bigger share

questions.explanation: In "1 in N", a bigger N means a smaller share. 1 in 2,600 is ten times the chance of 1 in 26,000.
